title: AI companies destroy old books to train AI. Here's why.
excerpt: There's a backlash against book destruction — and a better way to scan them.
content_html:
The AI industry, not content with alienating top creators, seems to be intent on alienating book lovers too.

That much is clear in the wake of a 404 Media report on ISBNdb, a company that tracks book data and briefly offered "AI training data" in the form of "the world's largest book database."

So far so normal; AI companies looking to build better AI models are hungry for fresh data from any source that isn't the internet. Books — generally better edited and more cogent than your average Reddit thread — make AI sound smart. (There's a premium on books published before 2022, ironically because we can't be sure if books were written by AI after that date.)

But on a now-deleted page, ISBNdb also advertised a "legally-binding nondisclosure agreement" that would hide an AI company client's "identity and strategy." Why? ISBNdb explained: "Destroying millions of books evokes images of burning libraries ... the optics problem is real. 'AI company destroys two million books' is not a headline that generates sympathy."

Indeed. Turns out ISBNdb was offering destructive book scanning, an industrial process that claims to turn pages into data faster than the "move a page, take a picture" alternative — by slicing the spines off books and feeding the pages into a scanning machine, photocopier style, then recycliny them. (ISBNdb's now-deleted advice: "lead with the recycling story, not the destruction story."

But if you just recoiled with horror at the destruction story, you're not alone. It wasn't a headline so much as an impassioned pro-book post from a financial newsletter that caught the internet's attention last week.

Among the post's 2,000 outraged replies was one from Elon Musk, pledging that Grok's book training would be done the "hard way" in the case of rare books.

Though as commenters quickly pointed out, Musk offered no definition of what was a "rare book" — nor any promise that his AI company would avoid destroying books in other cases.

This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.

As for ISBNdb, the company has belatedly walked back its destructive book offerings. "We've chosen to pivot away from that direction," the company's news site now says. The service was a "test of market interest." ISBNdb assured users it hadn't so much as scanned a single book.

But ISBNdb isn't alone. AI-feeding book destruction has happened before, and if the rare books sales spikes also noted in the 404 are to be believed, it may be happening again, right now, with other vendors under other nondisclosure agreements.

All while other less-destructive book scanning options — with less risk of messing up the scanned text — are widely available.

Mashable Light Speed

Which AI companies are destroying books?

It has long made sense to train Large Language Models on books. At first, that meant books legally online or in the public domain, such as the contents of Project Gutenberg. But rivalry between OpenAI, Anthropic, and other LLM builders led to a growing temptation to use online collections of pirated books.

We may never know whether OpenAI gave in to that temptation. In 2024, a class-action lawsuit from the Authors Guild found that the company had deleted the database of books it used to train its GPT models, and no one who worked on the database still worked at OpenAI.

But Anthropic was caught, and has admitted to using millions of pirated books to train Claude. That class action lawsuit, in which a record $1.5 billion copyright settlement was just approved, also revealed the scale of Anthropic's physical book-destruction operation.

Anthropic "became convinced that using books was the most cost-effective means to achieve a world-class LLM," wrote U.S. District Judge William Alsup in a lengthy legal order dated June 2025.

The company was "not so gung-ho" about using pirated material from 2024 onwards, to quote a memorable internal email in evidence, but still wanted to train Claude on "all the books in the world."

The result was called Project Panama. Alsup explains: "Anthropic spent many millions of dollars to purchase millions of print books, often in used condition. Its service providers stripped the books from their bindings, cut their pages to size, and scanned the books into digital form — discarding the paper originals."

As a matter of law, Alsup found this book mutilation was "transformative" and fell under the definition of fair use — because of the IRL book destruction, they were effectively exchanging one real-world copy for one digital copy. If Anthropic had ignored pirated databases, bought physical books from the start, then torn them apart in this manner, the authors wouldn't have a case.

But as a PR matter, Alsup's order was a disaster for Anthropic — generating exactly the sort of "AI company destroys millions of books" headlines that ISBNdb was offering to reframe. In court documents, one vendor boasted of its "hydraulic powered cutting machine" and how a recycling company would pick up the remnants.

Is there a better way to scan books?

This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.

The scale and speed of Project Panama, by all accounts, were astonishing. Other court documents say Anthropic sought a vendor to "convert from 500,000 to two million books over a six-month period."

To put that in perspective, around 2 million new books were published each year (again, before the 2022 AI slop book cutoff point). Scanning a year's worth of books via six months of slicing and dicing is a pace at which nondestructive book-scanning methods might struggle to keep up.

Nevertheless, in a world where we're still haunted by Nazi book burnings, as well as by classic dystopian novels of book destruction (Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451, George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four), it is the more sensitive nondestructive scanners that maintain the moral high ground.

Take the Internet Archive, a nonprofit that preserves the internet (including those deleted ISBNdb pages) via the Wayback Machine. The archive has been scanning books for years, and in 2021, a tweet about its nondestructive Scribe scanner, above, went viral — in a good way.

The Archive has experimented with scanners where robots turn pages, but found it didn't work for rare books. Instead, every page is turned by hand. The operator in the viral tweet, one of 70 Scribe workers, said she had scanned roughly 18,000 books in 10 years.

As the Scribe was going viral, the Archive celebrated uploading its 2 millionth book — but it had taken 20 years to get there (and would soon face a copyright lawsuit of its own). Sadly, there's no way it can keep pace with a book-slicing automated document feeder.

Instead, it's possible the only thing that might keep AI companies from chopping up books at a rate that would make Bradbury and Orwell spin in their graves is the same thing that made IBSNdb back down: the spotlight of public attention.

content_html_zh:
人工智能行业并不满足于疏远顶尖创作者，似乎也有意疏远图书爱好者。

404 Media 对 ISBNdb 的报道清楚地表明了这一点，ISBNdb 是一家跟踪图书数据并以“世界上最大的图书数据库”的形式简要提供“人工智能培训数据”的公司。

到目前为止还算正常；寻求构建更好的人工智能模型的人工智能公司渴望从互联网以外的任何来源获取新鲜数据。 书籍——通常比普通的 Reddit 帖子编辑得更好、更有说服力——让人工智能听起来很聪明。 （具有讽刺意味的是，2022 年之前出版的书籍价格较高，因为我们无法确定该日期之后的书籍是否是由人工智能编写的。）

你可能也喜欢

但在现已删除的页面上，ISBNdb 还宣传了一份“具有法律约束力的保密协议”，该协议将隐藏人工智能公司客户的“身份和战略”。 为什么？ ISBNdb 解释道：“销毁数百万本书让人想起图书馆被烧毁的景象…… 光学问题确实存在。 ‘人工智能公司销毁了 200 万本书’并不是一个能引起同情的标题。”

的确。 事实证明，ISBNdb 正在提供破坏性的书籍扫描，这是一种工业过程，声称可以比“移动页面、拍照”的替代方案更快地将页面转换为数据——通过将书脊切下来并将页面送入扫描机（复印机风格），然后回收它们。 （ISBNdb 现已删除的建议：“以回收故事为主导，而不是破坏故事。”

但如果你只是对这个毁灭性的故事感到恐惧，那么你并不孤单。 这与其说是一个头条新闻，不如说是上周引起互联网关注的一份金融时事通讯中热情洋溢的支持图书的帖子。

该帖子收到了 2000 条愤怒的回复，其中一条来自埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk)，他承诺，对于善本书籍，Grok 的图书培训将以“艰难的方式”进行。

尽管正如评论者很快指出的那样，马斯克没有给出什么是“稀有书籍”的定义，也没有承诺他的人工智能公司将避免在其他情况下销毁书籍。

至于 ISBNdb，该公司迟来地收回了其破坏性的图书产品。 该公司的新闻网站现在表示：“我们选择偏离这个方向。” 该服务是“市场兴趣的测试”。 ISBNdb 向用户保证它连一本书都没有扫描过。

但 ISBNdb 并不孤单。 人工智能喂养的图书销毁事件以前曾发生过，如果 404 中提到的珍本图书销量激增可信的话，那么现在这种情况可能会再次发生，而且是根据其他保密协议与其他供应商发生的。

与此同时，其他破坏性较小的书籍扫描选项（弄乱扫描文本的风险较小）也已广泛使用。

可混搭光速

哪些人工智能公司正在销毁书籍？

长期以来，在书籍上训练大型语言模型一直是有意义的。 起初，这意味着合法的在线或公共领域的书籍，例如古腾堡计划的内容。 但 OpenAI、Anthropic 和其他法学硕士建设者之间的竞争导致使用在线盗版书籍的诱惑越来越大。

我们可能永远不知道 OpenAI 是否屈服于这种诱惑。 2024 年，作家协会发起的一项集体诉讼发现，该公司删除了用于训练 GPT 模型的书籍数据库，并且该数据库的工作人员已不再在 OpenAI 工作。

但人性被抓了，并承认使用了数百万本盗版书籍来训练克劳德。 该集体诉讼刚刚获得了创纪录的 15 亿美元版权和解协议，也揭示了 Anthropic 实体图书销毁业务的规模。

美国地区法官 William Alsup 在 2025 年 6 月发布的一份冗长的法律命令中写道，Anthropic“开始相信，使用书籍是获得世界级 LLM 的最具成本效益的方式”。

引用一封令人难忘的内部电子邮件作为证据，该公司从 2024 年起对于使用盗版材料“不再那么热心”，但仍然希望对克劳德进行“世界上所有书籍”的培训。

结果被称为“巴拿马计划”。 Alsup 解释道：“Anthropic 花费了数百万美元购买了数百万册印刷书籍，这些书籍通常处于二手状态。 其服务提供商将书籍从装订中剥离，将书页裁剪成合适的尺寸，并将书籍扫描成数字形式——丢弃纸质原件。”

从法律角度来看，阿尔苏普发现这本书的毁坏具有“变革性”，并且属于合理使用的定义——由于现实世界中的书籍被毁坏，他们实际上是在用一本现实世界的副本交换一本数字副本。 如果Anthropic忽视盗版数据库，从一开始就购买实体书，然后以这种方式将它们撕碎，那么作者就不会有案子。

但作为公关问题，Alsup 的命令对 Anthropic 来说是一场灾难——产生了 ISBNdb 想要重新构建的那种“人工智能公司毁掉了数百万本书”的标题。 在法庭文件中，一位供应商吹嘘其“液压动力切割机”以及回收公司如何拾取残余物。

有没有更好的方法来扫描书籍？

此推文当前不可用。 它可能正在加载或已被删除。

从各方面来看，巴拿马计划的规模和速度都令人震惊。 其他法庭文件称，Anthropic 寻求一家供应商“在六个月内将 50 万本书转换为 200 万本书”。

客观地说，每年大约出版 200 万本新书（同样是在 2022 年人工智能倾斜图书截止点之前）。 通过六个月的切片和切块来扫描一年的书籍是非破坏性书籍扫描方法可能难以跟上的速度。

然而，在这个世界上，我们仍然被纳粹焚烧书籍以及经典的书籍销毁反乌托邦小说（雷·布拉德伯里的《华氏 451 度》、乔治·奥威尔的《十九八十四》）所困扰，正是更灵敏的非破坏性扫描仪维持了道德制高点。

以互联网档案馆为例，这是一个通过 Wayback Machine 保存互联网（包括那些已删除的 ISBNdb 页面）的非营利组织。 该档案馆多年来一直在扫描书籍，2021 年，一条有关其非破坏性 Scribe 扫描仪的推文（如上图）以良好的方式疯传。

档案馆尝试过使用机器人翻页的扫描仪，但发现它不适用于善本书籍。 相反，每一页都是用手翻动的。 这条推文中的操作员是 Scribe 的 70 名员工之一，她说她在 10 年内扫描了大约 18,000 本书。

随着《Scribe》的火爆，Archive 庆祝上传了第 200 万本书，但它花了 20 年才实现这一目标（并且很快就会面临自己的版权诉讼）。 遗憾的是，它无法跟上书籍切片自动文档进纸器的步伐。

相反，唯一能阻止人工智能公司以让布拉德伯里和奥威尔在坟墓里旋转的速度砍书的因素可能就是让 IBSNdb 退缩的同一件事：公众关注的聚光灯。
